Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 32
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file
 Potential 3

src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 5
src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 23
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 5
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

Explanation

The application is setting the server port. To migrate a Java application that sets the server port to Azure Container Apps:

*Azure Container Apps allows you to expose port according to your Azure Container Apps resource configuration. For instance, a Spring Boot application listens to port of 8080 by default, but it can be set with server.port or environment variable SERVER_PORT as you need.
Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 25
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that has reached its End of OSS Support.
With the officially supported new versions from Spring, you can get the best experience. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose a supported Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and determine the most suitable supported Spring Boot version.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Your application is using a Spring Framework version that has reached its End of OSS Support.
Upgrading to a supported version ensures better performance, security, and compatibility with modern tools.
1. Pick a Supported Version: Review the Spring Framework support policy and choose an actively supported version.
2. Update Your Project: Change the Spring Framework version in your pom.xml or build.gradle.
3. Fix Compatibility Issues: Update deprecated code, replace removed features, and ensure dependencies are compatible with the new Spring Framework version.
4. Thoroughly Test: Run unit, integration, and end-to-end tests to make sure everything still works after the upgrade.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single-module Java 8 Spring Boot application providing a browser-based photo gallery, uploads, detail navigation, deletion, and image delivery. The diagrams describe the checked-in implementation and Docker Compose topology, not a verified running deployment; credentials are intentionally omitted.

Application Architecture

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle is the sole production data store identified in the inspected application code and configuration. Photo maps UUID identifiers, filenames, MIME type, size, timestamp, dimensions, and a byte-array LOB to photos; uploads persist bytes in the database and /photo/{id} returns them rather than reading an uploaded file from disk. The /uploads/ path retained in metadata is compatibility information, not the image-serving path. Compose mounts oracle_data for Oracle files and an initialization directory, connects the two services through photoalbum-network, and starts the application after the database health check succeeds. Both application profiles set spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create, so persistent database storage does not imply preservation of application tables across application starts. The browser loads Bootstrap assets from jsDelivr; no backend remote API, cache, or message broker is identified. H2 is a test-scoped dependency, not a production database.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-108; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-179; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:23-83; docker-compose.yml:10-50; src/main/resources/application.properties:17-25; src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:13-17; pom.xml:88-93.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Layered monolith with constructor injection: three MVC controllers depend on the PhotoService interface; its transactional implementation depends on PhotoRepository. Templates, JSON upload results, and binary image responses share one application process. Evidence: HomeController.java:23-32,37-97, DetailController.java:17-27,32-78, PhotoFileController.java:22-38, and PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-48 under src/main/java/com/photoalbum/.
  • Database-backed media with Oracle coupling: image bytes and metadata live together; native repository queries use Oracle features such as ROWNUM, NVL, and TO_CHAR, rather than a database-neutral repository alone. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:36-41; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:16-100.
  • Public reads, authenticated mutations: the security filter chain requires authentication for POST /upload and /detail/*/delete, permits other requests, uses stateless HTTP Basic, and disables CSRF. The admin account is built in memory with BCrypt from externalized configuration; no credential values are reproduced here. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:28-61.

API & Service Communication Contracts

The application defines five controller endpoints: two HTML reads, one binary image read, one multipart-to-JSON upload, and one deletion action. Browser requests and downstream persistence calls are synchronous; no application messaging or remote business-service API clients were found.

Evidence references below are workspace-relative source paths and line numbers. This is a static source assessment, not a runtime verification; credential values are intentionally omitted.

API Endpoints Inventory

Service / ControllerMethodPathRequest TypeResponse Type
photoalbum-java-app / HomeControllerGET/No explicit parametersNormally 200 HTML, Thymeleaf index view; model contains List and a timestamp. A retrieval exception is caught and renders the same view with an empty list.
photoalbum-java-app / HomeControllerPOST/uploadAuthenticated multipart request; required repeated part files, bound as List200 JSON Map containing overall success and per-file success/failure lists, including when all processed files fail; explicit 400 JSON for a null/empty bound list. Missing required part can be rejected by Spring binding with 400 before controller entry. Unauthenticated requests receive a Basic challenge / 401.
photoalbum-java-app / DetailControllerGET/detail/{id}String path parameter idNormally 200 HTML, Thymeleaf detail view with Photo and previous/next identifiers. Missing photo, blank ID, or caught exception returns redirect:/ (normally 302), not 404.
photoalbum-java-app / DetailControllerPOST/detail/{id}/deleteAuthenticated request; String path parameter id; no request-body DTOredirect:/ (normally 302) for success, missing photo, or caught deletion error; outcome is carried by a flash attribute, not JSON. Unauthenticated requests receive 401.
photoalbum-java-app / PhotoFileControllerGET/photo/{id}String path parameter id; browser may append cache-busting _t query value, which the controller does not bind200 binary ResponseEntity backed by ByteArrayResource, using the stored MIME type; 404 for blank/unknown ID or absent/empty bytes; caught exceptions yield an empty 500 response.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37–98; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:18–78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:23–86; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:46–61; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:97–106,176–179. Binding-generated 400 and normal redirect statuses are framework behavior, not explicit ResponseEntity statuses in those handlers.

  • Versioning: no URL, header, or query-based API versioning is declared.
  • Upload outcome semantics: overall success means at least one photo was added to the successful response list. Clients must inspect both lists; HTTP 200 alone does not establish upload success. Each file is processed sequentially, followed by a lookup for successful uploads. An absent post-save lookup is silently omitted; a lookup exception is not caught by uploadPhotos and may yield framework-level 500 (HomeController.java:68–97).
  • Upload limits: configured multipart ceilings are 10 MB per file and 50 MB per request. There is no custom multipart-size exception handler in the inspected source, so no application-specific oversize error envelope is established. No controller/service enforcement of a maximum file count was found. Per-file service rejections become entries in the 200 JSON response rather than 400 responses. Constraint details belong in business-workflows.md. Evidence: src/main/resources/application.properties:23–30; PhotoServiceImpl.java:82–109,138–154,181–189.
  • Image headers: successful binary responses set Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private, Pragma: no-cache, Expires: 0, and X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, X-Photo-Size (PhotoFileController.java:74–83).
  • Framework/static surface: /css/, /js/, and bundled /uploads/** resources are additional static content, not controller APIs. /error is a potential Spring Boot default error dispatch, not a custom management endpoint. No custom global error handler or standardized error DTO was found.

Communication Patterns

  • Inbound and internal synchronous calls: browser navigation/forms and fetch('/upload') call MVC handlers. Controllers invoke PhotoService directly; PhotoServiceImpl invokes PhotoRepository synchronously through JPA/JDBC. The repository is an in-process component, not a separate network service. Database access is the implemented backend network boundary (HomeController.java:28–40,68–74; PhotoServiceImpl.java:28–30,53–75,172–185; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15–27).
  • Browser async is not messaging: the JavaScript upload function uses async/await, but it still makes one request/response HTTP call. No queue, broker, pub/sub, background processing contract, streaming API, or event subscription was identified (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:90–132).
  • Browser external dependency: templates load Bootstrap assets over HTTPS from jsDelivr. This is client-side static asset delivery, not an application-to-service business API (src/main/resources/templates/layout.html, index.html, detail.html).
  • No gateway aggregation: no gateway, BFF, remote REST/gRPC client, service registry, client-side load balancer, or downstream-service composition was found. Upload aggregation merely collects local per-file outcomes; detail-page composition joins the photo and adjacent-photo identifiers through local service calls (HomeController.java:58–95; DetailController.java:38–54).
  • Address resolution: the application connects to the Compose database service by the configured hostname oracle-db, using network DNS, not Eureka/Consul registration (docker-compose.yml:30–43; src/main/resources/application.properties:9–15). No additional service discovery mechanism is implemented.
  • Resilience and timeouts: no application-level retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback library, explicit HTTP client timeout, or explicit JDBC connection/query timeout was found. Dependency defaults are not asserted as application policies. Compose process restart-on-failure is not a request retry. Upload failures are converted into UploadResult; gallery read errors render an empty gallery; detail errors redirect; image-serving errors return 500; deletion errors redirect with feedback. No automatic retry occurs in the browser upload handler (PhotoServiceImpl.java:55–75,82–193,199–217; controller evidence above; docker-compose.yml:44; upload.js:102–132).
  • Availability prerequisite: Compose starts the app after the database is healthy; a required administrator password must also be supplied for security bean creation. Detailed startup/configuration mechanics belong in configuration-inventory.md, not this contract inventory (docker-compose.yml:35–41; SecurityConfig.java:33–42).
  • Authentication and authorization: stateless HTTP Basic authentication protects exactly POST /upload and POST /detail/*/delete. Other requests are permitted without authentication, including gallery and image reads. An in-memory user is assigned the ADMIN role and its password is BCrypt-encoded, but endpoint rules require only authentication, not an explicit role check. CSRF is disabled; no JWT/OAuth2, method-level role checks, or application TLS configuration was identified (SecurityConfig.java:28–61).
  • Transport and client behavior: the checked-in deployment exposes HTTP 8080; HTTPS termination is not demonstrated by the runtime configuration or Compose file. JDBC uses an Oracle thin connection without explicit TLS configuration. Browser code does not supply an explicit Basic Authorization header or implement a login flow; callers must arrange valid Basic credentials for mutations (src/main/resources/application.properties:1–15; docker-compose.yml:30–38; upload.js:102–106). No credential values are reproduced here.

Service Communication Sequence

The upload flow illustrates request authentication, local outcome aggregation, and the binary read that follows a successful upload. Dashed arrows represent responses, not queued events; no broker, gateway, retry, or circuit breaker exists in this flow.

sequenceDiagram participant Client as "Browser or API client" participant Security as "Security filter" participant Home as "HomeController" participant Service as "PhotoServiceImpl" participant Repo as "PhotoRepository" participant DB as "Oracle database" participant Image as "PhotoFileController" Client->>Security: POST /upload multipart files with Basic credentials alt Authentication missing or invalid Security-->>Client: 401 Basic challenge else Authenticated Security->>Home: uploadPhotos List of MultipartFile alt Bound file list empty Home-->>Client: 400 JSON success false and error else Files present loop Each file sequentially Home->>Service: uploadPhoto MultipartFile alt File rejected Service-->>Home: UploadResult failure else File accepted Service->>Repo: save Photo Repo->>DB: JDBC insert alt Save completes DB-->>Repo: Stored photo Repo-->>Service: Photo Service-->>Home: UploadResult success with photo ID Home->>Service: getPhotoById Service->>Repo: findById Repo->>DB: JDBC select DB-->>Repo: Photo Repo-->>Service: Optional Photo Service-->>Home: Optional Photo else Save throws within handled block Repo-->>Service: Exception Service-->>Home: UploadResult failure without retry end end Home->>Home: Collect successful metadata and failure entries end Home-->>Client: 200 JSON success and outcome lists end end Client->>Image: Public GET /photo/id Image->>Service: getPhotoById Service->>Repo: findById Repo->>DB: JDBC select DB-->>Repo: Photo bytes or absent Repo-->>Service: Optional Photo Service-->>Image: Optional Photo alt Photo and bytes found Image-->>Client: 200 image bytes with no-store headers else Missing photo or bytes Image-->>Client: 404 else Caught retrieval or response-building exception Image-->>Client: 500 without retry end

Diagram evidence: HomeController.java:55–97, PhotoServiceImpl.java:69–75,82–193, PhotoFileController.java:37–86, and SecurityConfig.java:46–61. The successful post-save lookup is shown; its absent-result/uncaught-exception edge cases are described in the endpoint inventory. Exceptions raised later at transaction completion can likewise escape the service's internal save catch; the diagram does not imply every persistence failure is converted to a normal JSON outcome.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Compose interpolation → required environment inputs: ORACLE_PASSWORD, APP_USER_PASSWORD, and APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD use required-value interpolation; missing inputs prevent a normal Compose launch (docker-compose.yml:7,9,36). These are configuration gates, not service-readiness probes.
  2. Oracle container → initialization scripts: the initialization directory is mounted into the image’s startup hook location. create-user.sh validates required credential variables and sleeps 30 seconds before issuing SQL; this is a fixed delay, not a retry/readiness loop (oracle-init/create-user.sh:9-22). The numbered SQL scripts configure/verify a fixed schema identity; custom APP_USER values are not consistently reflected in those SQL files (oracle-init/01-create-user.sql:14-30; 02-verify-user.sql:4-12).
  3. Application → waits for → healthy Oracle: Compose depends_on.oracle-db.condition=service_healthy gates application startup (docker-compose.yml:39-41). The actual probe is the image-provided healthcheck.sh, interval 30 seconds, timeout 10 seconds, 15 retries, start period 180 seconds (docker-compose.yml:17-22). The mounted oracle-init/healthcheck.sql contains SELECT 1 FROM DUAL, but Compose does not explicitly reference it.
  4. Application context → datasource/admin configuration: Oracle datasource configuration and the required app.admin.password property must be available. Test startup substitutes H2/test properties. No application-container healthcheck, custom startup timeout, application readiness probe, config-server retry, discovery dependency, or TCP-wait utility is configured in the inspected sources.
  5. Azure script sequence, separate from Compose: existing Azure CLI login/subscription → resource group → ACR → AKS → ACR attachment → PostgreSQL server/database/firewall → server FQDN lookup → fixed 30-second wait → role/grant operations → generated .env (azure-setup.ps1:43-299). No application deployment/readiness gate is present in this script; successful infrastructure creation is not evidence that the application is running.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

  • Local Compose: operator copies .env.example to ignored .env and provides required passwords → Compose substitutes inputs → Oracle receives administrator/application credentials → initialization creates/configures the schema → application receives datasource and admin credentials through its environment. No secret-store fetch or application managed-identity authentication is configured (.env.example:1-17; docker-compose.yml:6-9,30-36).
  • Application security: Spring injects app.admin.*; the configured password is BCrypt-encoded for an in-memory user store (SecurityConfig.java:28-42). BCrypt is password hashing, not encryption of .env or environment values. The test profile supplies its own redacted credentials.
  • Azure provisioning: caller must already have Azure CLI access; the script checks the active account (azure-setup.ps1:43-50). PostgreSQL administrator/application passwords come from optional process environment variables or a cryptographic-RNG helper with default length 24 (azure-setup.ps1:15-22,38-41). Administrative credentials are passed to Azure CLI for provisioning/SQL; application credentials are persisted in plaintext to ignored .env (azure-setup.ps1:117-127,203-257,274-299). AKS is attached to ACR for image-pull access (azure-setup.ps1:99-105); this is not a database secret-binding mechanism. No Kubernetes Secret creation, Key Vault binding, database managed-identity setup, or application deployment is shown.
  • Automation/tooling: GitHub workflow tokens support repository operations; the example MCP token entries belong to developer tooling. Neither is shown supplying runtime application credentials.
  • Storage/access limitations: git-ignore protection is present, but no explicit .env permission hardening, secret rotation, encrypted property mechanism, or cloud secret-manager policy is configured in the inspected provisioning/runtime files. The Azure script writes .env rather than merging with the Oracle template, so local Compose secrets are not preserved by that generation step.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse a shared gallery, open individual photographs, and navigate by upload time. Authenticated users can add photographs in batches and permanently remove them.

Evidence references below use repository-relative paths and line ranges. This is a static analysis of the current implementation; no runtime behavior or external-service availability was tested. No credential values are reproduced.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhotoService / Photo collection managementA photograph with its original content and display information; the only persisted business entity found.Displayed in the shared gallery; earlier and later photos are derived from upload times, not explicit relationships. No album grouping or uploader ownership relationship is modeled.
UploadResult (operation result, not an entity)PhotoService / Upload processingCommunicates acceptance or rejection of one submitted file.A successful result references the created Photo; a failed result identifies the submitted filename and reason.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-108; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:6-29; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:220-237.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

The application has one local business service, not independently deployed domain microservices. Controller responsibilities are included to make orchestration boundaries explicit.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
PhotoService / PhotoServiceImplPhoto collection management: acceptance, storage, retrieval, ordering, deletionPhoto; produces UploadResultPhotoRepository and its database; local image-header readers for optional dimensions
HomeControllerGallery presentation and batch upload orchestrationNone; composes photo summaries and per-file outcomesLocal PhotoService
DetailControllerIndividual-photo browsing and removalNone; composes current and neighboring Photo referencesLocal PhotoService
PhotoFileControllerDelivery of stored photo contentNone; reads Photo contentLocal PhotoService
SecurityConfigAccess control, separate from the photo domainNo business entities; configures an in-memory administrative identityExternally supplied credentials; values intentionally omitted

PhotoRepository is the persistence boundary and the stored Photo is the source of truth for both content and metadata. There is no separate object-storage write or filesystem-write step in the upload workflow. The generated compatibility path is not the content-serving source.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:37-48,112-185; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-27; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:28-32,55-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:23-27,32-78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:28-83; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:28-61.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload a batch and publish accepted photos

Entry: A user selects or drops files in the gallery; the browser submits POST /upload. The protected write requires authentication.

  1. The browser applies Client upload screening, collects accepted files into one multipart request, and shows upload progress.
  2. HomeController applies Nonempty batch. It then calls PhotoService once per submitted file, sequentially.
  3. PhotoService applies Server file acceptance and Image dimension ceiling. It reads the content, derives optional dimensions, and assigns a compatibility filename/path.
  4. A new Photo receives its identity and upload time, then the service saves its content and metadata together. The result reports the new photo ID or a failure reason.
  5. For every successful result, the controller separately reloads the Photo and builds the gallery summary. Rejected files contribute to a separate failure list.
  6. The response aggregates successful summaries and failed-file messages. The browser prepends accepted photos to the gallery and shows any server-reported failures; each new image loads separately through the photo-content workflow.

Outcome and boundaries: This is partial-success processing, not an atomic batch: each service upload call has its own transaction. Overall response success means at least one summary was added. If a successful upload cannot be found on the follow-up read, it is omitted from the summaries without a corresponding failure entry. An exception from that follow-up read is not caught by the batch controller, so already completed file uploads can remain persisted even when the request fails.

Failure branches: Service-level validation or caught processing errors yield per-file failure results. Browser request/network failures yield generic upload feedback; no automatic retry or compensating deletion is implemented. Commit-time transaction failures can escape the method's internal save-error handling.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:48-132,135-179; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:55-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-29,82-192; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:93-107; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:46-61.

Workflow 2: Browse the gallery, inspect a photo, and navigate

Entries: Visitors open GET / and follow a photo link to GET /detail/{id}.

  1. HomeController requests the collection from PhotoService and renders the gallery using Chronological browsing.
  2. The gallery creates a detail link and a separate photo-content request for each photograph.
  3. DetailController applies Photo existence, loads the current Photo, then asks the service for the older and newer neighbors.
  4. The service queries upload times and selects the first matching photo in each direction. The detail view includes only the navigation links that have a neighbor.
  5. The detail page presents the original name, upload time, human-readable size, type, and available dimensions.

Degradation: A gallery retrieval exception is logged and replaced with an empty collection, making an unavailable collection look like an empty gallery. Blank/missing detail IDs, missing photos, and detail-loading exceptions redirect to the gallery; a neighbor-query exception also prevents the detail page from being returned.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37-49; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:53-75,223-237; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:22-56; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:81-113; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:62-132.

Workflow 3: Deliver a photograph for display

Entry: A gallery or detail image requests GET /photo/{id}.

  1. PhotoFileController applies Photo existence and loads the Photo through PhotoService.
  2. It checks for available stored content and returns those bytes with the Photo's recorded media type.
  3. The browser receives the original stored content, not a generated thumbnail or resized derivative. Responses discourage cached reuse so subsequent displays request fresh content.

Degradation: Blank IDs, unknown photos, or missing/empty content yield not found. Other exceptions yield a server error. There is no alternate content source or placeholder fallback in this controller.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:94-95; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:65-70.

Workflow 4: Confirm and permanently remove a photograph

Entry: A user confirms the detail-page delete form, submitting POST /detail/{id}/delete; authentication is required.

  1. The browser asks for confirmation; cancellation prevents submission. This confirmation is presentation behavior, not a server-side approval rule.
  2. DetailController delegates removal to PhotoService.
  3. The service checks existence. A missing Photo returns false; an existing Photo is deleted from the database, including its stored content as part of the same entity.
  4. The controller redirects to the gallery with a success, not-found, or generic failure flash message.

There is no soft-delete lifecycle, recovery operation, separate file cleanup, or ownership-based eligibility check in this flow.

Evidence: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:64-78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:198-217; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:54-60.

Other entry-point findings: No scheduled business tasks, message/event listeners, command-line business runners, or startup domain-state initialization were found in src/main/java. The application entry point only starts the application. Repository methods for month filtering, pagination, and statistics exist but are not invoked by the inspected service/controller workflows, so they are not treated as exposed business processes.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:58-100; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:50-237.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no backend-to-backend domain-service calls, gateway aggregation, event choreography, or circuit breakers in the inspected application. The business context communicates through local controller-to-service-to-repository calls.

  • Batch composition: HomeController joins each accepted UploadResult to a reloaded Photo using the returned photo ID, then combines summaries with failed-file results. PhotoService and the database provide all business data; no remote domain is consulted.
  • Detail composition: DetailController combines the current Photo with older/newer photo IDs derived from the same collection by timestamp. This is local composition, not a cross-service join.
  • Presentation/content split: Pages and upload responses carry photo identity and display information. The browser subsequently requests content by the same identity. The compatibility upload path is not used to retrieve the actual content.
  • Unavailable dependency behavior: Database listing failures become an empty gallery; detail failures redirect; content failures return a server error; caught upload failures become per-file rejections; deletion failures become flash feedback. No secondary database, remote fallback, durable retry, or compensation is implemented in these paths.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:44-86; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-185,198-237; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:172-179.

Business Workflow Sequence

Primary workflow: upload a batch, publish successful items, and display their stored content. Error branches below reflect implemented decisions, not a hypothetical circuit breaker.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Acceptance and validation

  • Client upload screening: The browser accepts JPEG, PNG, GIF, or WebP MIME types and at most 10 MiB per file. Accepted files may proceed even when other selected files fail screening. Empty file collections are ignored by the browser; empty files are rejected by the server. Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-87.
  • Nonempty batch: A null or empty bound file list produces a bad-request response. The controller does not implement a file-count ceiling. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:57-68.
  • Server file acceptance: The service lowercases the submitted content type and checks the configured allowlist, rejects content larger than 10,485,760 bytes, and rejects zero-length content. A missing content type causes the outer generic-error path rather than a dedicated type-validation response. Content-type acceptance is not equivalent to verifying that the bytes are a decodable image. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:86-110,186-190; src/main/resources/application.properties:28-29.
  • Image dimension ceiling: When an image reader recognizes the content, width multiplied by height must not exceed 40,000,000 pixels. Header inspection avoids full image decoding. No recognized reader means upload can proceed without dimensions; an IOException rejects the file, while other dimension-extraction exceptions are logged and processing continues. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:34-35,122-158.
  • Declared Photo constraints: Original and stored filenames must be nonblank and at most 255 characters; the compatibility path is at most 500 characters; file size is required and positive; MIME type must be nonblank and at most 50 characters; upload time is required. These are entity validation declarations, not explicit controller prechecks. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:28-79.
  • Configured versus implemented limits: Multipart configuration limits individual files to 10 MB and requests to 50 MB. A setting specifies ten files per upload, but no consuming Java check was found; it must not be described as an enforced ten-photo business limit. Evidence: src/main/resources/application.properties:24-30; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:57-91; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:37-48.

Ordering, identity, and lifecycle

  • Chronological browsing: Gallery order is newest first. Previous means an earlier upload, choosing the first descending-time result; next means a later upload, choosing the first ascending-time result. Timestamp comparisons are strict, so photos sharing the same timestamp are excluded as neighbors; there is no explicit tie-breaker or wraparound. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:22-56; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:223-237.
  • Photo existence: Blank detail IDs redirect; absent detail photos redirect. Content requests with blank/unknown IDs or unavailable bytes return not found. Deleting an absent Photo returns false. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-42; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-62; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:199-205.
  • Identity and derived values: New Photos receive generated identities and the current local upload time. Compatibility filenames are independently generated with the original extension; dimensions are optional derived information. Display sizes are calculated from stored byte size. Duplicate-content detection and original-filename uniqueness checks are not implemented in the traced upload flow. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:93-107; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-170,243-249; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:114-125.
  • Lifecycle: Submitted file → rejected result or persisted Photo → permanently deleted Photo. These are observed operations, not a stored status enum or approval state machine. No draft, moderation, retention, or restore workflow is present in the inspected domain/service. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-108; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:82-217.

Transactions, errors, logging, and authorization

  • Transactions and integrity: PhotoServiceImpl is transactional, with read-only overrides for reads and navigation. Each controller-invoked upload is a separate service transaction; the batch controller has no enclosing transaction. Content and metadata belong to one Photo, so there is no cross-store synchronization or bidirectional business relationship maintenance. Caught save failures return a result inside the method, but transaction flush/commit may still fail at the proxy boundary; per-file failure reporting is not guaranteed for every persistence error. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-29,53-75,160-192,223-237; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:55-97.
  • Error handling: Upload errors normally become UploadResult failures; read/delete service errors are wrapped as runtime exceptions and handled as described in the workflows. No domain-specific exception hierarchy, saga, dead-letter queue, or automatic retry appears in these paths. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:55-75,150-190,199-217; controller evidence cited above.
  • Business logging: Upload acceptance/rejection, database errors, missing/deleted photos, and content delivery are logged. Content delivery additionally logs a small byte prefix. These application logs are not a modeled business audit trail; the Photo has no uploader or deletion-history relationship. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:91-102,179-189,201-216; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:45-72; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-108.
  • Authorization: Gallery, details, and photo content are publicly readable. Upload and deletion require authentication through stateless HTTP Basic. A configured identity has the ADMIN role, but the route rules check authentication, not that role; no per-photo ownership rule exists. CSRF protection is disabled. Credential values are intentionally omitted. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-61; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-108.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The declared baseline is Spring Boot 2.7.18 and Java 8 (pom.xml:8–13,23–26), an older stack outside Spring Boot's community support window. A Boot 3 upgrade requires Java 17 or later and consideration of the Jakarta namespace transition, particularly for the JPA, validation, and security stack. Commons IO is explicitly pinned to 2.11.0 rather than left to parent management; review its current advisories and compatibility before retaining that pin. The unresolved Oracle driver version prevents an evidence-based driver support assessment. No vulnerability scan or dependency resolution was performed, and no specific CVE findings are asserted here.

Notable Observations

  • Eight of nine non-test dependencies rely on parent-managed versions; the two test dependencies do as well. A parent upgrade therefore affects most of the declared dependency set (pom.xml:30–101).
  • spring-boot-starter-json is directly declared despite its “Image processing” comment; the declared artifact is a JSON starter, not evidence of a dedicated image-processing library (pom.xml:75–79). Potential overlap with the web starter cannot be quantified without the external dependency graph.
  • DevTools has optional=true but no runtime scope, so its declared scope defaults to compile. Optionality controls downstream propagation; it does not itself establish exclusion from the packaged application (pom.xml:95–100).
  • org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-maven-plugin is declared without a version (pom.xml:103–109); its inherited version was not resolved. No standalone messaging, caching, logging, or observability dependencies are directly declared; this does not imply their absence transitively.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The data layer contains one JPA entity, Photo, persisted through Spring Data JPA/Hibernate to Oracle, with H2 substituted for the test profile. Image bytes and metadata share the same table; there is no separately mapped album or user entity.

Data Ownership Boundaries

  • Store topology: One application module owns one configured datasource and the photos table. Base and Docker profiles target Oracle; the test profile substitutes an isolated in-memory store. There is no evidence of independently owned database-per-service boundaries or a database shared by multiple application services in the inspected implementation.
  • Access boundary: Controllers consume PhotoService, which accesses the database through PhotoRepository. No cross-service data retrieval, direct access to another service's tables, or gateway aggregation enablers were found (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:28-40; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:28-46; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:37-47,53-75).
  • Read/write semantics: Reads and writes use the same entity, repository, and datasource; no separate CQRS read model, event sourcing, replication routing, or outbox is present. Read-only transaction annotations do not establish a separate read store.
  • Payload ownership: Image bytes are authoritative in the relational BLOB; generated filename and path are compatibility metadata. Metadata and payload consequently share transaction and deletion boundaries (PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-124,160-174,198-210).
  • Record ownership: No user/tenant foreign key or per-photo owner field exists. The admin principal is maintained in memory rather than a domain table (Photo.java:15-91; SecurityConfig.java:33-42).
